name: Tundra folk
one_line: No tree for a hundred miles, so the lamp was the hearth: a bowl of seal fat that heated, lit and cooked, in houses of snow, sod and whalebone.

needs: a shore, a river crossing or a char river within a day's walk
a bank to dig the autumn house into

staples: seal (the lamp's fat and the winter's meat)
whale and walrus where the shore allows
seabird eggs, crowberry and bog bilberry in the short summer
how: the fish_run here is the sea and the crossing: seals harpooned at the breathing hole and the floe edge, the char run, the caribou swimming the river in autumn
a stone weir across the char river, the fish speared with a three-pronged leister
caribou lanced from a skin kayak as the herd swims the crossing, turned there by lines of stone figures
the big skin boat (umiak) for the whale
preserve: dried on racks in the wind (nikku)
cached under stones on the permafrost: the ground is the freezer
fermented under stones on the shore (igunaq): summer meat that ripens over autumn and freezes for winter; done wrong it kills
fat rendered and kept in skin bags for the lamp

fuel.note: the real hearth is the lamp: rendered seal or whale fat in a soapstone bowl (fat_lamp) gives heat, light and cooking from one flame, so for tundra folk the lamp IS the fire and the woodpile is a fat store. A fire, when there is one, burns driftwood off the tide line on the coast and dried dung and dwarf-willow brush inland. On the sea ice nothing burns but the lamp.

shelter.form: three houses a year: a dome of snow blocks in winter, a sod-and-whalebone house (qarmaq) dug a metre into a bank in autumn and spring, a skin tent in a ring of stones in summer; a low tunnel entrance as a cold trap, a raised sleeping platform, the lamp in the middle

TUNDRA.fuel: dung and dwarf-willow brush; driftwood where the shore is near; the lamp does the rest
TUNDRA.food: caribou at the crossing, char at the weir, eggs and berries in the short summer
TUNDRA.shelter: the sod-and-whalebone qarmaq dug into a bank; a skin tent in a ring of stones on the moss
TUNDRA.palette: lichen grey-white, moss green, sod brown, whalebone ivory

SEA_ICE.fuel: nothing burns; the lamp alone, fed by the seal it lights
SEA_ICE.food: seal at the breathing hole and the floe edge; char through a hole in the ice
SEA_ICE.shelter: the snow house of the winter sealing camp, blocks cut from wind-packed drift (no camp is placed on the ice: a tundra camp walks out to it and back)

knows: Arctic cottongrass heads and dried moss for the lamp wick; sphagnum for wadding and the house's cracks
crowberry and bog bilberry, and that crowberries keep under the snow
willow leaves and sorrel eaten green against scurvy (raw meat and fat did most of that work)
reindeer lichen: where it grows the herd will come
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why the old house pits grow the greenest grass on the tundra; which grass the wick is made of
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: cottongrass and moss for the wick; the berries that hang under the snow; willow and sorrel to eat green

techniques.name: Fat lamp
techniques.verb: a soapstone bowl, rendered seal fat, a wick of cottongrass or dried moss laid along the rim and trimmed with a stick so it does not smoke
techniques.teaches: the headman's technique because for these folk it is the fire itself: with no tree within a hundred miles, one flame gave heat, light, cooking, melted snow and dried the clothes; the women tended it and never let it go out
techniques.unlocks: a light that burns for hours and does not blow out; set it down inside a shelter

techniques.name: Dung fires
techniques.verb: gather dry caribou and musk-ox dung, and dwarf willow with it
techniques.teaches: fuel where there are no trees; the summer fire outside the tent, while the lamp carries the winter
techniques.unlocks: dung and brush in the fire pit; a camp's fuel store inland

techniques.name: Hide
techniques.verb: scrape the skin with a bone scraper, chew and work it soft, cut it with the half-moon knife, sew with sinew and a bone needle in a stitch that keeps water out
techniques.teaches: clothing is what let people live where nothing grows; every warm thing the player could wear comes from here: the parka, the kamik boots, the kayak's skin
techniques.unlocks: the camp sews parkas, boots and skin covers; the player wears what the maker makes

techniques.name: Snow and sod
techniques.verb: cut wind-packed snow into blocks and spiral them into a dome; dig into a bank and roof it with whale ribs, sod and skins; pitch a skin tent in a ring of stones
techniques.teaches: shelter where there are no trees: the low tunnel is a cold trap, the sleeping platform sits above the cold, and the lamp glazes the snow walls to ice
techniques.unlocks: the camp's three houses, one a season; the winter sealing camp out on the ice

techniques.name: Stone cache
techniques.verb: pile fitted stones over meat and fish on the permafrost so fox and bear cannot get in; the cold does the rest
techniques.teaches: the tundra's storage, the hinge of the ladder: a surplus you cannot keep is rot, and here the ground is a freezer
techniques.unlocks: food keeps through the dark; the player can cache food under stones and come back for it

techniques.name: Stone figure
techniques.verb: stack stones into a figure that reads at a distance: this way, a cache here, the crossing is there
techniques.teaches: a mark that stands in the place of a person; a line of them turns a caribou herd, and a chain of them is a road across land with no landmarks
techniques.unlocks: the player can raise a waymark that persists and reads along the road

ladder: the lamp lit in a skin tent: a hearth that needs no tree
the seal, the char weir and the crossing: the fish_run
the stone cache and the drying rack: meat keeps through the dark
sewn skins, sinew and ivory go along the coast; driftwood and soapstone come back
growth.restraint: the hunt takes the crossing's share and lets the herd pass; the cache is filled, not the river emptied; one whale feeds a village for a winter and its bones become the house; dung and willow are gathered, never stripped, because the lamp carries the winter
growth.ceiling_hint: a whaling shore (a whale a year) reaches the tribal ceiling in whalebone houses; an inland crossing feeds a band; a bare coast stays a family or two

signatures.what: a ring of stones in the moss where a skin tent's skirt was weighted; a small hearth of stones to one side
signatures.restore: cleared: the summer tent goes up on the old ring

signatures.what: oval hollows a metre deep with a low tunnel toward the shore; the greenest grass on the tundra grows in them
signatures.restore: restored: the camp re-roofs the old pit with skins over the old bone
signatures.inherits: the walls and the frame: the autumn house in a week

signatures.what: a rib or jaw arch standing alone on the shore, ivory-white, where a roof was
signatures.restore: cleared: raised again as the frame of the sod house roof
signatures.inherits: the roof frame, which no tundra grows

signatures.what: a low cairn of fitted stones, hollow inside: the fox-proof larder
a stone figure on a rise, still standing; a line of them leads to the crossing or the cache
signatures.restore: restored: the fallen ones re-stacked so the line reads again
signatures.inherits: the road: waymarks to the crossing, the weir and the cache

ruin.plants_differ: sod-house pits and old middens grow the lushest grass and sedge on the tundra: nitrogen and phosphorus from bone, blood and fat, still measurable in the ponds beside whalebone-house villages four hundred years after they emptied; the rest of the tundra is lichen, moss and dwarf shrub

aesthetic.silhouette: low domes and mounds that barely break the horizon; a whale-rib arch; a rack of split fish; a stone figure on the rise; a kayak on its stand
sounds: the herd's hooves at the crossing

real_world.region: Arctic Canada, Greenland and Alaska; a living people
real_world.note: a soapstone lamp burning seal (or whale) blubber with a wick of Arctic cottongrass or dried moss lit along the rim and trimmed with a taqquti; tended by the women, it heated, lit and cooked for the tent, the qarmaq and the snow house, melted snow and dried clothes; older than the Inuit themselves (the Dorset people, the Tuniit, burned soapstone lamps from c. 500 BCE) and on Nunavut's coat of arms today

real_world.analogue: Inuit: clothing and the hide craft
real_world.note: caribou-skin parkas and sealskin kamik boots; skins scraped, worked and chewed soft, cut with the ulu, sewn with sinew from the caribou's back and needles of bone; a year's clothing was a year of women's work, and it is what let people live where nothing grows

real_world.region: Arctic Canada and Greenland, c. 1000–1600 CE
real_world.note: oval houses of stone, sod and whalebone dug a metre down, a sunken cold-trap entrance, a roof of bowhead ribs and jaws; given up for the snow house as the Little Ice Age cooled, while the qarmaq (a low wall of stone, sod or snow, a whalebone frame, skins over, moss in the cracks) stayed the autumn and spring house into the 1950s; the whale bones and waste still enrich the ponds and grass around the pits

inuksuk: 'that which acts in the capacity of a human'; stone markers for routes, fishing places, camps, caches and sacred sites, and in lines as drift fences to turn caribou; the human-shaped inunnguaq is only one kind; Inuksuk Point on Baffin Island holds more than a hundred

summer walrus, seal, caribou or birds buried under stones near the shore to ferment through autumn and freeze through winter, eaten the next year; the cold does the preserving, and done wrong it can kill (botulism)

real_world.region: south-west Alaska, St Lawrence Island and Chukotka; a living people
real_world.note: sod houses, the qasgiq men's house and the ena beside it, sometimes joined by a tunnel; spring and summer at fish camp for salmon and seal, winter at the village; the seal-oil lamp (naniq) the furniture of the house

real_world.analogue: Nenets (and the Sámi): a herd note
real_world.region: Yamal and the Russian Arctic; Sápmi in Fennoscandia; living peoples
real_world.note: reindeer herders of the tundra-taiga edge, not sea folk: the conical skin tent (chum) on poles, migrations of hundreds of kilometres a year, the reindeer giving meat, hide, sinew and draught; wood carried north as the trees run out — the herd fundamental belongs to the taiga file, this one keeps the sea
